name: Dana Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Riverside Growers, which is a co-operative farm owned by its members, about forty of us, though only six work there full time. We've got pigs, four hundred laying hens and a few hectares of vegetables we sell in boxes to people in town. I start at seven with the hens, then the pigs, then whatever's on the board. I'm the newest, two years in, and I still can't back a trailer to save my life.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty years behind a pharmacy counter, counting pills and listening to people's troubles. My knees and my back are fine but my head was bored stiff. Now I use the AI on my phone all day long, honestly: I ask it why the hens are pecking each other, I get it to plan the veg box rota, I photograph a weed and it tells me what it is. The others laugh at me, then come and ask me to ask it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, oh, that's a shame, and people would look at me funny. I'd say it on the co-op group chat and at the members' meeting. I was rather hoping it would take the heavy lifting off us, and if it doesn't, that's a missed chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, nothing much changes, I'd still be using it to plan the rota and identify weeds. I'd be a bit disappointed for the farm, though. The pig muck isn't going to shovel itself, and Pedro's back is already bad at forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on using the phone tools every day, and maybe push the co-op to get a cheap egg-counting camera if it actually works. Nothing changes with money, we've got Mark's wage, my pharmacy savings and the house. I'd probably try to learn the trailer properly instead, the old-fashioned way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little flat. Like a party that ended early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So you were hoping for more change than this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. I've read about weeding robots that zap weeds with a little laser, and we spend whole days on our knees in the carrots. I'd have loved to see one on our rows before I retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it odd to be disappointed that your own job stays safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think it is, for me. The robots I want are the ones that do the jobs nobody wants. I'm not asking for a machine to chat to the pigs, I'm asking for one to clear the muck.

S0.say: I'd say that's a shame, and people would look at me funny. I was hoping it would take the heavy lifting off us, and if it doesn't, that's a missed chance.
S0.think: For me nothing much changes, and I'd still use it every day for the rota and weeds. I'd be disappointed for the farm, because the pig muck won't shovel itself.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools on her phone daily and pushes the co-op to try a cheap egg-counting camera. Leaves money plans alone and works on learning to back a trailer the old way.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a party that ended early.
S0.quote: I'm not asking for a machine to chat to the pigs, I'm asking for one to clear the muck.
S0.fieldNote: Dana is the rare farmer who'd be disappointed that AI stays small. She sees the tools as relief for hard, dirty work rather than a threat to her. Her worry for others, like a colleague with a bad back, already shows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure the machines work for the people doing the work, not just the people who own the land. At the members' meeting I'd say, we're a co-op, we can buy the weeding robot together and share what it saves. Online I'd probably start a long thread about it and regret it by teatime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of it, which feels a bit guilty to say. I'm the one already using these tools. If a robot comes to the farm, somebody has to set it up and argue with it, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd ask the co-op board to look at a weeding robot for the carrots and a camera for the hens, and I'd offer to run a trial for one season. I'd do a short course on farm robots at the agricultural college, there's an evening one I've seen. And I'd bring the farmworkers' union in early, so the younger staff get trained and nobody's hours are cut without a vote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite excited, with a bit of guilt mixed in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the co-op would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pedro, he's 40 with a bad back and three kids, and he's brilliant with the pigs but hates anything on a screen. And Lou, who's 22 and does most of the veg. I'd want them both trained before anything gets bought, or I'd vote against it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put money in. How much would you actually put up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eight thousand from savings. I've got more than that sitting in the bank doing nothing. I'd put it in as a member loan to the co-op, on the condition the savings go into wages and not just into the reserve.

S1.say: I'd say this is the moment to make sure the machines work for the people doing the work, not just the landowners. As a co-op we could buy the weeding robot together and share what it saves.
S1.think: I think I'd do well out of it, which feels a bit guilty. I already use these tools, so if a robot comes, I'm the one who sets it up and argues with it.
S1.do: Asks the co-op board to trial a weeding robot and a hen camera for a season and takes an evening course on farm robots. Brings the union in early, insists two colleagues are trained first, and offers about 8,000 from savings as a member loan.
S1.feel: Calm and quite excited, with some guilt mixed in.
S1.quote: If a robot comes to the farm, somebody has to set it up and argue with it, and that's me.
S1.fieldNote: She becomes the person pushing the farm forward, and money from her savings goes in on conditions. Her progressive views shape how, not whether: shared ownership, union involvement, training first. She names her guilt about doing well openly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big question isn't the robots, it's who owns them. If three companies own all of it, we're in trouble, and I'd say that loudly, at the members' meeting and online. I'd be calling for public ownership of the big models and for co-ops to get help buying the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'm 58 with savings, and I'd probably enjoy the robots. What would keep me up is the idea of my kids, the twins, being 30 and having nothing to do and nobody owning anything except a few men in another country.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, before it arrives, I'd get the co-op to buy what it can while there's still a market for small buyers, and put my own money into that. I'd go to every meeting of the regional co-op federation and push for a shared machinery pool, the way farmers used to share a combine. Once it arrives I'd probably step back from the farm work and help run the pool, since that's the bit I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, for how it all gets shared out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Only two years of warning here. What does that short window change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It takes away the time to do it fairly. You can't set up a machinery co-op in two years and get a law passed and train people. You'd end up with the big estates buying everything first and the rest of us paying them to rent it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be thinking about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The twins. Jo's a lab technician and Sam drives a forklift in a warehouse. I'd tell them both to take the time now to figure out what they love doing, because work may not be what pays the bills any more, and I'd say we can help with money if it comes to that.

S2.say: I'd say the big question isn't the robots but who owns them. I'd call loudly for public ownership of the big AI systems and help for co-ops to buy the machines.
S2.think: I'd be fine personally at 58 with savings, and I'd probably enjoy the robots. What would keep me up is my children having no work while a few men abroad own everything.
S2.do: Gets the co-op to buy what machines it can before the big buyers take the market and puts her own money in. Pushes the regional co-op federation for a shared machinery pool, then steps back from farm work to help run it.
S2.feel: Uneasy, not about herself but about how everything gets shared out.
S2.quote: You'd end up with the big estates buying everything first and the rest of us paying them to rent it.
S2.fieldNote: Her personal position is strong, so her unease is about power and ownership. She's the only kind of person who would rush to buy the robots for her workplace in the fastest picture. Two years is too short for the shared, fair version she wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get it right if we start now, and I'd mean right now, this winter. I'd say co-ops and public ownership loudly, same as before. I'd also tell people to try the tools now so they're not frightened of them later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's actually ideal. I'd be 63, I'd have time to get the co-op's robots running, and then I could hand over and retire with my head up. My worry for the twins doesn't go away, it just gets five years of breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the season trial at Riverside next spring and build from there, one machine a year. I'd join the federation's committee and help set up the shared machinery pool properly, with rules. And I'd sit down with Mark and plan to stop full time at 62 or 63 and stay on as the robot person two days a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, a bit excited, and actually rather hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you use those five years for, beyond the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching. I'd want to run little sessions for older farmers, the ones like old Henrik at the next farm who won't touch a phone, so they're not left behind. Half of it is just showing people it's not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the twins to change jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not now, I'd say, but I'd tell them to start learning the tools in their own jobs. Sam's warehouse will go fully robotic well before 2031. I'd rather he be the forklift driver who becomes the robot fixer than the one at home.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get it right if we start this winter. Co-ops and public ownership, same as before, and I'd tell people to try the tools now so they aren't frightened later.
S3.think: For me it's ideal: at 63 I'd have time to get the co-op's robots running and then retire with my head up. My worry for my children gets five years of breathing room.
S3.do: Starts a season trial at the co-op next spring and adds one machine a year. Joins the federation committee to set up a shared machinery pool, and plans to cut to two days a week at 62 or 63 as the farm's robot person.
S3.feel: Calm, busy, excited and rather hopeful.
S3.quote: I'd rather he be the forklift driver who becomes the robot fixer than the one at home.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is her sweet spot: enough time for the fair, shared version she wants and a dignified exit. She wants to teach older neighbours, showing her generosity. Her advice to her son mirrors her own late switch into something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no one should be caught out, and the government should start retraining money now rather than in year nine. I'd say it, then I'd hear people say there's no hurry, and I'd get cross. Ten years has a way of becoming two if everyone waits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Personally, I'd be retired before it fully arrives. I'd be 68. I'd honestly be a little sad to miss the best of it on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still start the trials at Riverside next year, because the hard jobs are hard now, not in 2036. I'd do the robotics evening course, help set up the shared machinery pool, and then retire at 63 or so as I'd planned. Money stays as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit impatient with everyone else, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would say that with ten years there's no rush. What would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I suppose they're right. But you know, I came to farming at 56 because I was bored stiff. I'd hate to see people waste ten years being frightened when they could be learning something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you see yourself still involved after you retire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, in a pottering way. I'd keep a few hens and an AI on my phone telling me why they're pecking each other, same as now.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so nobody should be caught out, and retraining money should start now, not in year nine. Ten years has a way of becoming two if everyone waits.
S4.think: I'd be retired before it fully arrives, at 68. I'd honestly be a little sad to miss the best of it on the farm.
S4.do: Starts robot trials at the co-op next year anyway, because the hard jobs are hard now. Takes the robotics evening course, helps set up the shared machinery pool and retires around 63 as planned.
S4.feel: Calm, and a bit impatient with people who think there's no hurry.
S4.quote: Ten years has a way of becoming two if everyone waits.
S4.fieldNote: The long runway makes her impatient rather than relaxed, and she would act on the same timetable regardless. She'd miss the most interesting part, which shows how much she welcomes it. Her retirement picture still includes hens and an AI tool.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of who'd end up owning everything. The robots themselves don't scare me, I'd welcome them in the muck shed tomorrow. What would help is public money for co-ops and small farms to buy machines together, and laws so the big AI systems are owned or at least tightly controlled by the public.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether older people can learn this stuff. I'm 58, I left school at sixteen and I'm the one on the farm who talks to the machine. The idea that it's only for the young ones is rubbish, and it stops a lot of people my age from even trying.

headlineQuote: I'm 58, I left school at sixteen and I'm the one on the farm who talks to the machine.
portrait: Dana Fischer is 58 and spent thirty years behind a pharmacy counter before joining Riverside Growers, a member-owned co-op farm with pigs, hens and vegetables. She's still learning the practical side but uses AI tools all day and has become the person colleagues ask to check the machine. She'd welcome robots for the hard, dirty jobs and would put her own savings into buying them through the co-op. Her unease in the fast AGI picture is about ownership, not her own job: she fears a few companies owning everything while her children's generation has no work. She stays calm in the slower pictures and sees five years as the best case.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because a handful of companies and big estates would end up owning all the machines.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for co-ops and small farms to buy machines together, and laws putting the big AI systems under public ownership or tight public control.
